newsitem.title: USA: Congressional analyst - USDA ag estimate too bullish.
newsitem.headline: Congressional analyst - USDA ag estimate too bullish.

text.p: An agricultural analyst with the Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday the Agriculture Department's estimates for 1997/98 crop demand and prices are a little on the bullish side.

Speaking at the department's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum, David Hull said he feels USDA analysts are projecting slightly too high growth rates in developing nations, and that demand may not be as strong as USDA is anticipating.
"USDA has very hot growth (estimates) in low income countries," said Hull. "Their estimates are not off the charts, but it's at the top edge for almost everybody, and all at once."
Hull said CBO estimates for average prices for major U.S. crops through 2000 at lower levels than USDA projections, due largely to lower disappearance estimates by the CBO.
CBO puts corn prices a few cents lower than USDA estimates for the next couple of years, then 10 percent lower by 2000.

Wheat prices are estimated 10 percent lower, then 20 percent lower after the year 2000. CBO soybean prices are four percent lower than USDA forecasts in nearby years and drop to 15 percent below after 2000.

In defending the lower price and demand projections, Hull noted for example that in China, which is expected to be a key market for U.S. commodities in the coming years, urban consumers are already spending 50 percent of income for food and rural consumers are already spending 60 percent. He said higher commodity prices could "tend to mitigate what demand will do."
